items.title: Line current — 100 MVA at 132 kV, 0.9 pf
items.stem: A three-phase transformer is rated 100 MVA, 132 kV. The specification also states 0.9 power factor. What is the HV line current to use for winding and bushing checks?
items.why: Line current follows apparent power: I = S / (√3 × U). Power factor scales watts, not the ampere rating at a given MVA.

options.label: 437 A — I = 100 MVA / (√3 × 132 kV). The 0.9 pf does not change line current at this MVA.
393 A — use P = 90 MW so I = 90 MW / (√3 × 132 kV).
758 A — I = 100 MVA / 132 kV (treat as single-phase).
218 A — divide the three-phase current by 2.

items.title: OLTC / AVR limitation on a weak 132 kV bus
items.stem: An automatic voltage regulator is hunting on a weakly interconnected 132 kV bus. The on-load tap-changer is already on the last raise tap, yet the bus is still below target. What is the correct engineering limitation?
items.why: An OLTC only relocates voltage within its tap range. It is slow mechanical regulation, not a reactive-power source. Once the raise end-stop is reached the AVR must stop stepping; further voltage support is a system (VAR / tap of another unit / operator) problem.

options.label: Refuse further raise commands. The OLTC cannot create voltage beyond the tap range; leave the AVR from hunting and call for reactive support.
Keep the AVR in auto — it will find a tap beyond the nameplate range if the bus stays low.
Block the AVR but run the tap-changer in manual raise past the last tap, because mechanical stops are conservative.
Treat the OLTC as a STATCOM analogue: tap faster to supply VArs into the weak bus.

items.title: YNd11 — what the clock number actually fixes
items.stem: A specification calls for YNd11. Which statement is the engineering meaning, not a slogan?
items.why: YNd11 is HV star, LV delta, LV leading HV by 30°. The clock number is a phase-displacement constraint for paralleling and earth-fault behaviour — not a loss or impedance class.

options.label: HV star, LV delta, LV phasor at 11 o'clock relative to HV (LV leads HV by 30°).
Both windings delta; the '11' is an impedance code.
It is interchangeable with YNyn0 for paralleling because both are star.
The 11 is the number of OLTC steps.

items.title: GSU line current — 1,000 MVA at 400 / 21 kV
items.stem: A generator step-up transformer is rated 1,000 MVA, 400 kV HV / 21 kV LV. What HV and LV line currents do you use for bushing and winding checks? (Three-phase, line-to-line voltages.)
items.why: I = S / (√3 × U). At 1,000 MVA: HV ≈ 1.44 kA on 400 kV, LV ≈ 27.5 kA on 21 kV. Power factor does not change the ampere rating at a given MVA.

options.label: ≈ 1.44 kA HV and 27.5 kA LV — I = 1000 MVA / (√3 × U) on each winding.
≈ 27.5 kA HV and 1.44 kA LV — the generator side is always the smaller current.
Scale both currents by 0.9 pf because machines are specified at lagging pf.
I = S / U so HV is 2.5 kA and LV is 47.6 kA (omit √3).
